stem: A 47-year-old woman with hypertension comes to a large academic center clinic where interns and residents frequently rotate. The patient was diagnosed with hypertension several years ago but did not follow up and was not taking any medication. She went to the emergency department 2 weeks ago due to chest pain, which was determined to be of musculoskeletal origin and was treated symptomatically. The patient's blood pressure was found to be 160/100 mm Hg, and outpatient follow up was arranged. She is now feeling well and has no symptoms. Current blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg and pulse is 80/min. BMI is 26 kg/m2. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. Long-term complications of hypertension without adequate control are explained, and the patient agrees to take antihypertensive medication. Which of the following is most likely to improve treatment adherence in this patient?

options.A: Bringing a family member or friend to most appointments
options.B: Charging fees for missed appointments
options.C: Discussing alternative, nondrug, no-cost therapies
options.D: Providing free medication samples when initiating a new drug
options.E: Seeing the same physician for most office visits

explanations.A: Bringing a family member or friend to appointments might reinforce the patient's understanding of the disease and treatment, but relying on others to address medication adherence can add to family care burden and exacerbate interpersonal conflict. Also, it is often not practical to bring a companion to appointments.
explanations.B: Charging fees for missed appointments can reduce no-show rates but can discourage patients from scheduling follow-up appointments. In addition, the fees can contribute to friction between patients and physicians, further undermining rapport.
explanations.C: Although drug cost can be a barrier to adherence, in this case, medications cannot be avoided due to the severity of hypertension and presence of end-organ damage. The impact of cost on adherence can be minimized by prescribing inexpensive generic antihypertensives when appropriate.
explanations.D: Medication samples are intended primarily to allow patients to quickly test new medications for effectiveness and tolerability. However, samples tend to encourage the use of expensive, nongeneric medications, which can complicate efforts at long-term adherence.

Physicians can build rapport with patients by actively listening, showing understanding of the patient's concerns (including nonmedical concerns), and maintaining open communication with the patient. Once good rapport/trust has been built, patients are often more willing to share specific reasons for poor adherence, such as cost concerns, complexity of regimen, or embarrassing adverse effects.
educationalObjective: Arrangements should be made for patients to be seen by the same physician for most visits to establish good rapport and improve adherence with the medical regimen.

stem: During a particularly busy winter season, the medical director of a primary care clinic implements a strategic plan to reduce iatrogenic transmission of respiratory viruses among patients and staff within the clinic. As part of the plan, all clinic staff complete an in-service training on infection control and influenza vaccine counseling practices; additional dispensers of hand sanitizer are installed in prominent, high-traffic areas; and an updated ventilation system is installed to improve air circulation. In addition, patients in the waiting room are provided masks if they are experiencing cough or fever, and all eligible patients receive enhanced counseling and educational materials promoting influenza vaccine administration. This strategic plan best represents which of the following approaches to increase safety?

options.A: Automating high-risk action
options.B: Incorporation of "hard stops" against incorrect action
options.C: Overlapping barriers to block safety hazards
options.D: Repeated cycles of process improvement

explanations.A: Computerized automation can reduce errors in high-risk, manually performed processes (eg, automated calculation of drug infusion rates with an infusion pump). None of this clinic's interventions involve automation.
explanations.B: Forcing functions, also known as "hard stops," use physical design to prohibit incorrect action. For example, oxygen and nitrous oxide gas containers can be designed with different, incompatible connectors, which eliminates accidental connections to the wrong cylinder. Forcing functions are not seen in this clinic.
explanations.D: Continuous quality improvement methods, such as the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle, seek to improve a process by repeatedly testing, measuring, and refining a test of change. This clinic's interventions are implemented concurrently rather than sequentially or cyclically.

generalExplanation:
The Swiss Cheese Model (SCM) is a strategy often used in health care organizations to increase safety. SCM recommends overlapping multiple barriers (visualized as slices of cheese) within a process to block hazards. Targeted hazards include both internal human error (eg, mistakes resulting from fatigue) and external threats (eg, infectious agents).

SCM is based on the following principles: e No single defensive barrier (eg, handwashing) is fully error proof; each intervention contains "holes" or vulnerabilities (eg, forgetting to wash hands, incorrect handwashing technique) that can enable an adverse outcome (eg, transmission of infection).

e« Harm occurs when hazards pass unchecked through holes in defensive barriers.

e Stacking multiple, overlapping "slices" or defensive barriers increases the likelihood that hazards will be detected early and downstream harm (ie, adverse patient outcome) will be blocked.

In this clinic, overlapping barriers against virus transmission include interventions targeting human effort (eg, masks, hand hygiene stations), medical care (eg, vaccination), and the physical environment (ventilation systems). These barriers in combination are more effective in reducing transmission of infection than each barrier alone.
educationalObjective: The Swiss Cheese Model (SCM) recommends overlapping multiple barriers to increase system safety. SCM depicts each defensive barrier as having vulnerabilities (akin to holes in a slice of cheese); therefore, stacking together multiple interventions (ie, layers of cheese) can block hazards (eg, error caused by fatigue; infectious pathogen) from passing through the system to cause harm (ie, adverse patient outcome).

stem: A 36-year-old man has been hospitalized for the past 3 days for alcoholic hepatitis. His condition is slowly improving and his prognosis is favorable. However, this is his third absence from his job in the past 6 months due to health-related issues. The patient notified his employer that he is presently hospitalized and was informed that he needs to provide the employer with proof of hospitalization or he could lose his job. In accordance with hospital policy, the patient provides verbal consent for the physician to speak with his employer and disclose his health status. The employer proceeds to contact the physician directly by phone, requesting an update on the patient and his likelihood of returning to work. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician to the employer?

options.A: "I can confirm that the patient is currently hospitalized, and I anticipate he will be able to return to work."
options.B: "I can disclose information to you only in the presence of the patient, so we need to schedule a meeting."
options.C: "I cannot discuss a patient's care with anyone without a written signed release of information."
options.D: "I cannot verify your identity and therefore cannot disclose any information about the patient."
options.E: "The diagnosis is alcoholic hepatitis and I expect him to recover and return to work in the coming days."

explanations.B: If prior authorization for disclosure has been given, the patient's presence is not required.
explanations.D: HIPAA does not require the provider to obtain proof of identity of phone callers before speaking with them. However, in some cases, a health care provider or hospital may establish additional rules for verification of a phone caller's identity.
explanations.E: Acentral aspect of the HIPAA privacy rule is the principle of "minimum necessary" disclosure. The physician should disclose only the minimum amount of protected health information needed to respond to the specific request. In this case, the physician is asked to confirm that the patient is hospitalized and comment on his likelihood of returning to work. The physician does not need to disclose the patient's diagnosis to the employer and should avoid doing so as this sensitive information could jeopardize the patient's future employment.

generalExplanation: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) privacy rule outlines the handling of protected health information. The main goal is to protect patients' privacy and confidentiality. A physician can respond to an employer's request for health information only if the patient has specifically provided verbal or written authorization for release of information to the employer. Because this patient has given his physician verbal permission to speak with his employer and discuss his care, in accordance with hospital policy, the physician can provide this information. In general, a written (rather than verbal) release of information document is preferred to protect both the patient and physician from any misunderstanding, but this is not a HIPAA requirement (Choice C).
educationalObjective: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act protects health information by requiring verbal or written authorization for release of information. Hospitals and physicians' offices frequently have additional policies requiring written forms for release of information and procedures to verify the identity of phone callers. It is important that health care providers be familiar with these rules and disclose only the minimum necessary information.

stem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the emergency department experiencing severe lower back pain. The pain began 4 weeks ago and is getting progressively worse. At night, the pain has become so severe that it awakens her from sleep. The patient has tried over-the-counter ibuprofen with no relief of symptoms. She also reports feeling more tired than usual but says, "It is probably because my kids are home for the holidays and are keeping me busy." The patient has a history of breast cancer that has been in remission for 2 years. Her physical examination is significant for weakness and numbness of the left lower limb. Radiographic findings are consistent with metastatic lesions in her spine. Which of the following is the most appropriate next statement in initiating a conversation about this patient's condition?

options.A: "Have you considered the possibility that your pain is due to metastatic disease?"
options.B: "Have you considered whether or not you want to know the cause of your condition?"
options.C: "l am sorry but the examination suggests the cancer may have returned. I can imagine this is devastating news."
options.D: "I am sorry to tell you that the cancer has possibly spread, but we can treat you aggressively with radiation and chemotherapy."
options.E: "What is your understanding about what might be causing your back pain?"

explanations.A: Immediately stating the likely diagnosis without any preparation or assessment of this patient's perception is not an optimal way to begin the discussion. Using simpler vocabulary rather than medical terms such as "metastatic disease" may also be preferable.
explanations.B: Physicians should generally determine how much the patient wants to know. However, beginning the discussion this way suggests bad news and would likely raise this patient's anxiety level, especially if she has not considered metastases as a possibility.
explanations.C: This approach delivers the news abruptly and then expresses excessive sympathy without allowing this patient to express her own emotions. This approach can engender hopelessness and hinder appropriate information exchange.
explanations.D: Stating that this patient likely has cancer in her back and then jumping straight to treatment options is insensitive and premature. The physician should pause after delivering bad news and allow the patient to express emotion and ask questions.

generalExplanation:
Breaking bad news is one of the most difficult situations a physician will encounter. A sensitive, patient-centered approach that is responsive to the patient's needs is preferred rather than expressing excessive sympathy or prematurely suggesting treatment options. An important first step is to find out how much the patient already knows and what the patient believes about his or her condition. This patient has a previous diagnosis of breast cancer, but to what extent she has been informed or understands her risk for metastatic disease is unclear. First listening to how the patient discusses her condition and fears will help the physician phrase the information accordingly. The physician can then communicate his or her suspicions and concerns in an empathic manner using language that is understandable to the patient, considering any religious or cultural issues, and adjusting the level of detail according to how much the patient wants to know.

Let the patient ask questions but do not overload him or her with too much information. Information may need to be repeated later after the emotion of the situation has been absorbed. educationalObjective: When delivering potentially bad news, a physician should first assess the patient's comprehension, fears, and desire for information to deliver the news in an empathetic yet comprehensible manner.

stem: A 16-year-old girl comes to the office for an initial patient visit. Medical conditions include asthma and mild acne. The patient maintains a B+ average at school. She does not smoke or use illicit drugs regularly but has tried alcohol and marijuana at parties a few times. She is not sexually active. When asked about extracurricular activities, the patient confides that she is thinking about quitting her high school softball team because "the other girls are mean, and I just don't enjoy playing anymore." When asked to describe how she feels, she hesitantly mentions that she gets depressed at times and frequently feels self-conscious and that no one likes her. The patient appears uncomfortable and nervously asks the physician. "You won't say anything about this to my parents, will you?" Which of the following is the most appropriate response to the patient?

options.A: Everything we discuss about your emotions, drugs, and sexual issues is just between you and me
options.B: Everything we discuss will be kept private with a few exceptions as required by law
options.C: | will not volunteer any information but must respond truthfully if your parents ask any questions about your condition
options.D: It's good that you're talking about what's bothering you, but I am obligated to keep your parents informed because you are a minor
options.E: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act ensures that everything you say will be kept private

explanations.A: It is misleading to assure the adolescent patient of unconditional confidentiality. Situations involving risk of self-harm, homicidal ideation, or abuse require disclosure to the parents and/or state protective agencies.
explanations.C: The physician is not obligated to keep the parents informed or to respond to questions about what the adolescent discusses. The patient's confidentiality can be maintained if there are no exceptions.
explanations.D: The physician is not obligated to keep the parents informed or to respond to questions about what the adolescent discusses. The patient's confidentiality can be maintained if there are no exceptions.
explanations.E: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) does not ensure unconditional confidentiality for adolescents. HIPAA allows a physician to disclose information to a parent if required by state law.

generalExplanation:
Protecting the adolescent's confidentiality is important to maintaining a trusting physician-patient relationship and establishing an atmosphere of safety in which the adolescent feels comfortable discussing sensitive issues such as mental health, drug use, and sexuality. Adolescents are often unclear about the limits of confidentiality and are more likely to disclose sensitive information if the physician makes an explicit statement regarding confidentiality and its exceptions.

Adolescents should be informed that everything they discuss will be kept private with a few exceptions as required by law. Although state laws may vary to the extent which they protect the confidentiality of minors, most include the following exceptions: self-injurious or suicidal behavior, homicidal ideation, abuse, and neglect. Adolescents should also be informed that certain sexually transmitted diseases are reportable to public health departments.
educationalObjective: Having an explicit discussion about confidentiality and its exceptions is important to maintaining a trusting physician-patient relationship with adolescents. They should be informed that everything they discuss will be kept private with a few exceptions as required by law, which include suicidal or homicidal ideation, abuse, and neglect. stem: A 34-year-old man calls the office requesting an urgent appointment due to cough and cold symptoms. His temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), but he feels "miserable" and is unsure if he should go to work the next day. The patient has a history of seasonal allergies and knee pain from a past sports injury. He has no other medical problems but does have a history of frequent office visits. The receptionist informs him that the physician is preparing to leave as it is near closing time but that an appointment is available for the next morning. The patient declines the offer of an appointment and hangs up. As the physician leaves the office 30 minutes later to make evening rounds at the hospital, the patient arrives and insists on being seen immediately. He sounds congested and coughs occasionally but is breathing normally. He has no other symptoms. He again asks to be examined. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: "Although I understand your concern, we should address it tomorrow because it is not an emergency."
options.B: "l am sorry. I would normally see you, but I have another appointment that can't wait."
options.C: "l am sorry you drove all this way, but your problem can wait until tomorrow."
options.D: "I insist that you go to the nearest emergency department for evaluation."
options.E: "I regret that I cannot see you now; didn't my staff inform you that it is closing time?"
options.F: "Let me take a quick look; it's probably nothing to worry about."

explanations.B: This response suggests that the patient's behavior is appropriate and offers an excuse not to see the patient rather than explaining that non-emergency concerns can wait.
explanations.C: These responses set limits but are dismissive of the patient's concerns. It is better to acknowledge the concerns but explain that non-urgent issues are addressed during regular office hours.
explanations.E: These responses set limits but are dismissive of the patient's concerns. It is better to acknowledge the concerns but explain that non-urgent issues are addressed during regular office hours.
explanations.D: Recommending that the patient go to the emergency department for a non-urgent condition is inappropriate and places an unnecessary burden on emergency services.

generalExplanation: This physician is faced with a patient who inappropriately demands to be seen after hours for a non-urgent concern. A stable patient who fails to arrive at the appointed time should be advised to reschedule the appointment; the physician is under no obligation to immediately see this patient. Performing an examination after hours is inappropriate and reinforces the patient's sense of entitlement and poor boundaries. Acquiescing to the patient's demands would only encourage similar behavior in the future and create further tension in the physician- patient relationship due to the patient's lack of respect for the physician's time (Choice F). The most appropriate response is to calmly set limits and establish clear professional boundaries. The physician should explain in a polite yet firm tone that the examination will be deferred until the next day because the condition is not an emergency.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for follow-up after sustaining a ligament injury while playing football 4 weeks ago. The patient has been using a splint and going to physical therapy twice weekly. His pain has decreased, and he is hoping to return to football practice. Medical history is significant for asthma managed with as-needed albuterol and prior treatment of gonorrhea, which he acquired a year earlier after an unprotected sexual encounter. Physical examination of the ankle reveals no pain, tenderness, or swelling and there is full range of motion. At the end of the visit the mother mentions that the family is moving to a new neighborhood and will be changing medical providers. She asks for a copy of her son's medical record to take to the new practice. Which of the following is the best response to the mother's request?

options.A: Decline to provide the medical record but offer to exchange information verbally with the new provider
options.B: Explain to the mother that you are unable to provide the medical record because it is the legal property of the clinic
options.C: Inform the mother that you will transfer the medical records directly to the new provider
options.D: Provide only nonconfidential information to the mother
options.E: Provide the entire medical record to the mother because she has a legal right to it

explanations.A: Although the medical record is the property of the clinic, it is in the best interest of the patient to share information with new providers or specialists and inappropriate to decline the parent's request. The adolescent's confidentiality can be maintained by having the medical record transferred directly to the new provider.
explanations.B: Although the medical record is the property of the clinic, it is in the best interest of the patient to share information with new providers or specialists and inappropriate to decline the parent's request. The adolescent's confidentiality can be maintained by having the medical record transferred directly to the new provider.
explanations.D: Although redacting the record is a possibility, the mother has requested a copy of the record to facilitate continuity of care. Providing her with only nonconfidential information would maintain confidentiality but fail to adequately ensure continuity regarding the entirety of the patient's treatment history.
explanations.E: The mother does not have the right to the patient's entire medical record because confidentiality regarding treatment of STIs should be maintained.

generalExplanation: Protecting adolescent confidentiality is critical to maintaining open communication between the patient and physician regarding sensitive issues (eg, sexuality, mental health, substance use) and can significantly impact an adolescent's willingness to seek future health care. Adolescents have the right to consent for treatment of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and this information is considered confidential. In this situation, transfer of the medical record to the parent may inadvertently violate the patient's confidentiality regarding his treatment for gonorrhea. Rather than providing a copy to the parent, the patient's medical record can be transferred directly to the new provider. In this way, the mother's desire to ensure continuity of care is respected and the patient's confidentiality is not compromised.
educationalObjective: Adolescent confidentiality regarding sensitive issues, including treatment for sexually transmitted infections, mental health concerns, and substance use, should be protected. When transferring care, it is preferable to provide the medical record directly to the new provider rather than providing a copy to the parent.

stem: A 65-year-old heavy smoker with a lengthy history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the office due to recent-onset hemoptysis. He reports 3-5 episodes of coughing up blood in the past month. He also reports a 9.1-kg (20-Ib) weight loss in the past 2 months. Chest radiograph reveals a suspicious lesion, and a bronchoscopy followed by biopsy establishes the diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. When the patient is informed of his condition and the prognosis, he asks that no one in his family be told the news yet. He seems tearful but cognitively intact. His wife, who usually brings him to his visits and is also his health care proxy, calls the next day to inquire about the pathology report. She says she is deeply concerned because her husband is reluctant to discuss his condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Ask the wife to come to the office with a copy of the patient's health care proxy form.
options.B: In response to the wife's concerns, ask her to come to the office to further review the patient's status.
options.C: In response to the wife's concerns, inform her that the patient will receive comprehensive care.
options.D: Inform the patient that his wife must eventually be told if the patient refuses to do so himself.
options.E: Inform the wife of the pathology report results as she is his health care proxy.
options.F: Inform the wife that it would not be appropriate to discuss the patient's information.

explanations.A: The health care proxy is in effect only if the patient is deemed to have insufficient capacity to make decisions regarding his medical treatment (eg, delirious, nonresponsive). In this case it is not in effect, as there is no indication that the patient lacks capacity.
explanations.E: The health care proxy is in effect only if the patient is deemed to have insufficient capacity to make decisions regarding his medical treatment (eg, delirious, nonresponsive). In this case it is not in effect, as there is no indication that the patient lacks capacity.
explanations.B: Without the patient's permission, it would be inappropriate to reveal any information to his wife about his condition or care over the phone or in person.
explanations.C: Without the patient's permission, it would be inappropriate to reveal any information to his wife about his condition or care over the phone or in person.

generalExplanation: Health information cannot be shared with anyone (including family members) without the patient's permission. This patient's wishes must be respected and his confidentiality strictly maintained. That said, he should be strongly encouraged to discuss his diagnosis with his spouse as she will be significantly impacted by it. Moreover, she may be able to provide moral support to her husband, thereby easing his burden. The physician should encourage an open dialogue between the patient and his wife but should in no way coerce the patient to share the information (Choice D).
educationalObjective: Medical information should be shared with family members only with the patient's permission.

stem: A 26-year old woman comes to the emergency department due to 2 days of palpitations, shortness of breath, and anxiety. She has not had any chest pain or cough. The patient has a history of generalized anxiety disorder and takes sertraline and an oral contraceptive. She is sexually active with multiple partners, smokes 2 packs of cigarettes a week, and drinks 1-2 glasses of wine daily. On physical examination, the patient appears visibly agitated. Temperature is 37.6 C (99.7 F), blood pressure is 124/89 mm Hg, pulse is 102/min, and respirations are 18/min. Serum electrolytes, complete blood count, cardiac enzymes, and chest x-ray are within normal limits. ECG shows sinus tachycardia and is otherwise unremarkable. The provider reviews the patient's chart and notes that she was seen last week in the emergency department with an identical chief complaint. The assessment from this prior visit reads, "Given patient's history of generalized anxiety disorder, current symptoms likely represent panic attack." The provider decides that she is having a repeat panic attack. When the patient is about to be discharged, she suddenly enters cardiac arrest and cannot be resuscitated. Autopsy reveals multiple large pulmonary emboli. Which of the following factors most likely contributed to the missed diagnosis of pulmonary embolism in this patient?

options.A: Communication error
options.B: Documentation error
options.C: Framing bias
options.D: Information bias
options.E: Latent error eee

explanations.A: Communication error typically describes a breakdown in information relay, such as a change in clinical care or a lack of closed-loop communication within the medical team. In this scenario, there are no communication breakdowns to explain the patient's misdiagnosis.
explanations.B: Documentation error often occurs when information is omitted from the medical record (eg, not charting pertinent physical examination findings). There is no evidence of documentation error in this scenario.
explanations.D: Information bias describes the belief that more data is better, leading to overcollection of data, which can complicate efficient and accurate decision-making. In this case, the physician's cognitive bias resulted in collecting an insufficient, rather than an excessive, amount of data for diagnostic workup.
explanations.E: Latent errors are system-level factors, such as inefficient protocols or organizational structures, that cause adverse events. This case represents an active error (ie, relating to the physician's specific actions or judgement) caused by cognitive bias, rather than a system-level error.

generalExplanation:
Diagnostic errors (ie, missed or delayed diagnoses) are often caused by misinterpretation of clinical data, and account for up to 17% of hospital adverse events. They can arise from factors relating to the physician (eg, fatigue), the patient (eg, language barrier), or the system (eg, inefficient workflow). Diagnostic errors often result from cognitive bias, occurring when a physician's dependence on heuristics (ie, mental shortcuts) distorts clinical judgment and treatment.

This scenario illustrates several types of cognitive bias: e Framing bias occurred as the context of information (ie, medical record describing panic attack history and diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder) incorrectly limited the physician's "frame" of analysis. This bias led to the assumption that tachycardia, shortness of breath, and anxiety also represented a panic attack, rather than possible pulmonary embolism.

e Anchoring bias led to the physician fixating ("anchoring") on a presumptive diagnosis of panic attack without considering alternate causes.

e Confirmation bias resulted in the physician's oversight of information contradicting the presumptive diagnosis, including the patient's risk factors of smoking and oral contraceptive use.
educationalObjective: Diagnostic errors are commonly caused by cognitive bias, including framing, anchoring, and confirmation bias. Framing bias occurs when contextual information (eg, previous diagnosis) influences a physician's judgment, resulting in failure to consider alternate diagnoses.

stem: A 45-year-old man is seen in the clinic for follow-up of type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has attempted treatment with multiple oral agents but has experienced frequent hypoglycemia, and his glucose levels have remained uncontrolled. The physician prescribes a new, long-acting injectable antidiabetic drug that has a different mechanism of action than previous medications and does not cause hypoglycemia. However, 2 weeks later, the patient calls to report that his insurance company denied coverage because the medication was deemed medically unnecessary. Which of the following is the best next step by the physician?

options.A: Contact the insurance company to request medical director review
options.B: Counsel the patient to file an appeal with his insurance company
options.C: Explain that the patient must pay out-of-pocket for the medication
options.D: Refer the patient to a social worker to explore medication discount options
options.E: Request medication samples for the patient from the drug company

explanations.B: The initial appeal is best requested by the physician who understands the medical rationale for the requested medication. Placing the burden of appeal on the patient is less likely to be successful and increases the likelihood of inadequate treatment.
explanations.C: If the insurance plan denies coverage following review, the patient may need to pay the full cost out of pocket. However, the physician should first appeal for higher-level review.
explanations.D: Patients who cannot afford their medication often can obtain medications at discounted rates through charitable organizations or directly from the manufacturer through a discount program. However, these options are not necessary if the drug is approved following insurance review.
explanations.E: Medication samples are primarily intended to allow patients to quickly test new medications for effectiveness and tolerability. However, samples are not a dependable source of medication and should not be relied on as a patient's primary means of obtaining medication.

generalExplanation:
This patient has uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus and attempts at management with oral agents have led to frequent hypoglycemia. The physician prescribed a new, injectable medication that has a low risk of hypoglycemia (eg, GLP-1 agonist); however, the patient's insurance company denied coverage. Because the physician believes that this medication is appropriate therapy for this patient's condition, the physician should contact the insurance company to request escalated review.

Most insurance plans maintain hierarchical lists of medications based on cost-effectiveness to determine coverage. Preferred medications with the lowest cost and highest effectiveness (eg, metformin) are typically automatically approved for coverage; in contrast, medications that are more expensive (eg, nongeneric medication) or have elevated risk of adverse effects may require a higher patient cost share (eg, copay) or be denied coverage. However, patients sometimes require these nonpreferred medications. To address such circumstances, insurance plans maintain an appeal process (often termed prior authorization) in which a treating physician can request review from a physician (sometimes designated as a medical director or physician reviewer) or other qualified person (eg, pharmacist) who can review the patient's case and verify the appropriate need for the medication.
educationalObjective: Insurance plans may deny coverage of medications that are less cost-effective or carry higher risk than the preferred medication choices. When a treating physician believes a denied medication is appropriate therapy for a patient, the physician should request escalated review (eg, prior authorization) for coverage by the plan.

stem: A medical resident on call is asked to see a 72-year-old woman who has a headache. The medical record indicates that she was admitted 5 days ago after a fall that caused a hip fracture requiring surgical correction. The patient developed postoperative chest pain and was transferred to the medical service for further care. She is stabilized and receiving morphine for her pain but frequently calls nurses to say that she is uncomfortable. According to the nurse, the patient developed an intermittent headache earlier in the day that recurred an hour ago after her daughter called to say she would be unable to visit today. When she sees the resident, the patient snaps, "You look so young. I hope you know what you're doing." The resident asks a few questions about her headache, but she gives very little information. When the resident attempts to perform a basic physical examination, the patient yells, "Don't touch me. I'm going to complain to the hospital administrators about you because you have no idea how to properly deal with a patient." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: "As you may know, this is a teaching hospital; I can assure you that I am well trained and can consult an attending physician if necessary."
options.B: "l| am sorry you are unhappy with your care; you are free to file a complaint as described in the patient bill of rights."
options.C: "I see that you're upset; I imagine that you might be disappointed that your daughter was unable to visit."
options.D: "I see that you're upset; would you prefer to be seen by my supervising attending physician?"
options.E: "I understand that you are upset, but I can best help you if you allow me to proceed with the examination and make a diagnosis."
options.F: "May I ask what is upsetting you so that I can help you as best I can?"

explanations.A: Reminding the patient that she is in a teaching hospital and mentioning a lack of experience will likely further anger her and provide her with additional opportunities to criticize the resident.
explanations.B: Although patients have the right to file a complaint if dissatisfied with their care, suggesting this approach in a situation where there is no evidence of poor treatment is inappropriate and does nothing to resolve the issue or improve the physician-patient relationship.
explanations.C: Although the patient's disappointment that her daughter did not visit may be a contributing factor, it is inappropriate to assume this is the reason for her distress; this premature interpretation is likely to further aggravate the patient.
explanations.D: The best initial approach is to acknowledge the patient's distress and ask an open-ended question. It is likely that this situation can be resolved by the resident without involving the attending physician.
explanations.E: Although this patient's cooperation is necessary to complete the physical examination and make a diagnosis, her anger should be addressed first to facilitate her cooperation.

generalExplanation: This patient is irritable, angry, and verbally abusive to the resident physician. Although the immediate cause of her anger is unclear, her complicated medical course, general discomfort and pain, and probable disappointment that her daughter did not visit are likely contributing to her distress. Although the situation is challenging, it is the physician's responsibility to be nondefensive, defuse the patient's anger, and attempt to preserve the physician- patient relationship. Acknowledging the patient's distress, remaining nondefensive, and asking open-ended questions regarding what is upsetting the patient are the best means of establishing an open dialogue. Professionalism should be maintained at all times, and the physician should not retaliate with defensive or negative comments, which will only worsen the situation.
educationalObjective: When dealing with an angry patient, the most appropriate response is to remain nondefensive, acknowledge that the patient is upset, and begin the discussion with an open-ended question.

stem: A 28-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to a lump on his right arm. The patient reports, "It has been there for several years, but in the last few days, it has started moving and talking to me." He has a history of schizophrenia that has responded well to olanzapine. The patient has been admitted to the psychiatric floor twice in the last 12 months for psychosis due to medication nonadherence. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 156/92 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min, respirations are 16/min. On examination, the patient is alert and oriented to self, place, and time but keeps looking at his right arm and talking to it. The speech is pressured and confused at times. A soft, mobile, nontender, 2-cm mass is noted on the posterior surface of the right forearm. There is no surrounding warmth, erythema or fluctuance. The patient asks the physician to get close to it so he can hear it talk and again asks for it to be removed right away. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.A: Administer an antipsychotic medication and defer the request to remove the mass
options.B: Decline to perform the procedure and reassure the patient that the mass is benign
options.C: Obtain consent from the patient's next of kin prior to removing the mass
options.D: Remove the mass as requested by patient and administer an antipsychotic
options.E: Request a psychiatric assessment for decision-making capacity

explanations.B: Reassurance is unlikely to be effective, and it is inappropriate to ignore the patient's request indefinitely. Once his psychosis is treated, his decision-making capacity regarding surgical removal of the mass should be reassessed.
explanations.C: Obtaining consent from the next of kin as a surrogate decision-maker would be appropriate only if the situation were urgent and/or the patient's mental status were unlikely to improve. In this patient, removal of the mass is not urgent, and the patient's acute psychosis is likely to improve after he is prescribed antipsychotic medication.
explanations.D: This patient currently lacks capacity to consent for removal of the mass. His decision-making capacity needs to be reassessed once antipsychotic medication has taken effect, which may take days to weeks.
explanations.E: Capacity can be assessed by any physician who knows the risks and benefits of a treatment or procedure. In this patient, lack of capacity has already been established (ie, he is unable to understand his condition due to the influence of delusions and hallucinations). A psychiatric assessment for the purpose of assessing capacity is unnecessary.

generalExplanation: This patient with schizophrenia is acutely psychotic, and his thought process and judgment are currently influenced by delusions and hallucinations regarding his lump. Although he wants the lump removed, his reasoning is based on delusional ideas. For informed consent to be valid, a patient must demonstrate decision-making capacity. In his current condition, this patient lacks capacity because he is unable to understand his condition, appreciate the consequences of treatment options, or weigh the risks and benefits of the surgical procedure in a rational manner. When decision-making capacity is impaired by reversible factors (eg, psychosis, delirium), the next step is to treat the underlying cause with the goal of restoring decision-making capacity. In a nonurgent situation, as in this patient with a possible lipoma (eg, soft, mobile, nontender mass that has been present for years), the next step in management is to defer his request to remove the mass and treat his acute psychosis with the goal of improving his decision-making capacity.

stem: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 3, comes to the labor and delivery ward of a busy hospital in the active stages of labor. A team consisting of nurses, an attending physician, and a senior resident facilitate delivery of a healthy baby girl. The resident begins to repair a vaginal laceration and asks a third-year medical student, who is rotating with the team on the second day of an obstetrics and gynecology clerkship, to deliver the placenta. The medical student has only observed the delivery of a placenta once before, and hesitantly states that he is unsure whether he should perform the procedure independently. The resident states, "You've seen it done, so you should be able to do one by now." The student applies the clamp to the umbilical cord; however, as he gives traction, the cord tears, and the patient develops postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony and inability to deliver the placenta. Interventions addressing which of the following would most likely prevent future occurrences of this error?

options.A: Cognitive bias and judgement errors
options.B: Communication between physicians and nurses
options.C: Didactic instruction in obstetrics and gynecology
options.D: Fatigue and sleep deprivation
options.E: Teamwork and safety culture

explanations.A: Cognitive bias (ie, application of mental shortcuts in patient evaluation and treatment) can lead to incomplete differential diagnoses, delayed treatment, and diagnostic error. In this scenario, the adverse outcome reflects poor teamwork and communication, rather than biased diagnostic workup.
explanations.B: Interprofessional communication (ie, between team members of different professions, such as physician and nurses) improves teamwork and patient outcomes. However, it would not address the communication breakdown in this scenario between team members of the same profession (ie, medical student and senior resident).
explanations.C: Didactic training in obstetrics and gynecology addresses knowledge deficiency and may increase the student's theoretical understanding of the placental delivery procedure, but would not address inadequate team leader support during his first practical attempt.
explanations.D: Fatigue and sleep deprivation increase procedural error risk but are less likely factors in this medical student, who recently started a new rotation. Rather, the error is more closely related to poor leader responsiveness and subtle intimidation that pressured the student to deliver the placenta independently.

generalExplanation:
Teamwork, a foundation of safe medical care, is undermined by hierarchy-based barriers and intimidation. This team leader (senior resident) dismissed concerns of the junior team member (medical student), pressuring the student to perform a task above his skill level, which precipitated an adverse outcome. Behaviors of intimidation can be overt (eg, verbal outburst, throwing objects) or passive (eg, dismissiveness, impatience). In settings where leaders evaluate and supervise junior learners, intimidation can motivate junior team members to prioritize acquiescence and boldness over caution and patient safety.

Suboptimal team dynamics can be improved through teamwork training, including communication and mentorship, and promotion of safety culture (ie, shared prioritization of patient safety goals). Examples of relevant interventions include: e Teamwork simulation with teams practicing communication skills during simulated patient scenarios. e Safety debriefings consisting of collaborative, team-based discussion of patient safety risks and concerns. e Development of evaluation metrics rewarding members who identify errors and safety risks. Such interventions can improve communication skills of team leaders, increase psychological safety (ie, comfort in expressing safety-related concerns and asking questions) of junior team members, and improve leadership responsiveness.
educationalObjective: Hierarchy-based barriers and intimidation by team leaders can be active (eg, verbal outbursts) or passive (eg, condescension) and increases risk of adverse events. Teamwork and safety culture interventions (eg, simulation, debriefings) reduce error risk by improving team collaboration, leader responsiveness, and psychological safety of

stem: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, is brought to the emergency department by her husband due to heavy vaginal bleeding. She is at 30 weeks gestation by a last menstrual period and has not received prenatal care. The patient has had heavy vaginal bleeding for the past 2 hours, soaking through a pad every 30 minutes. Her last pregnancy ended in an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery at home. Vital signs and fetal heart rate tracing are normal. A transvaginal ultrasound reveals a complete placenta previa. After conservative management, the vaginal bleeding stops. The findings and management, including a cesarean delivery, are discussed with the patient and her husband. The patient says she does not want a cesarean delivery because she would like to deliver at home again. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: "A vaginal birth would be very dangerous, but if you understand and agree to these risks, I'll allow you to deliver at home."
options.B: "I will only recommend a cesarean delivery, because vaginal delivery puts your and your baby's lives at risk."
options.C: "I'll give you some time to discuss this with your husband, so you can make a decision about your preference together."
options.D: "We can discuss this again in a few days after you have had more time to weigh your options."
options.E: "You can have a vaginal delivery, but I recommend that you come to the hospital so we can help you if something goes wrong."

explanations.C: Deciding with her husband's help is an example of assisted decision-making, in which family or caregivers help the patient make decisions. Assisted decision-making is not required for this patient because her or her husband's preference for mode of delivery does not change the need for cesarean delivery.
explanations.D: Placenta previa can cause unexpected, often unprovoked, heavy vaginal bleeding, as in this patient's initial presentation. The risk of repeat hemorrhage is highest following an initial bleeding episode, and delivery decision-making should not be delayed in case another life-threatening bleed occurs.

Most medical decisions are made via shared decision-making, in which the patient's preferences and personal values are considered when discussing 22 medically reasonable treatment options. However, when there is only 1 medically reasonable treatment option that has clearly superior evidence-based support, it is ethically appropriate for the physician to provide directive counseling, in which a single treatment option is recommended to the patient.

This patient has a complete placenta previa, a condition in which the entire placenta covers the cervix, which is associated with a high risk of maternal (eg, hemorrhage) and fetal (eg, intrauterine demise) morbidity and mortality with vaginal delivery. Due to these risks, the only safe option for delivery is cesarean delivery. Although this patient prefers a vaginal delivery, it is inappropriate for the physician to discuss this choice as a safe and reasonable option (Choices A and E). It is the physician's ethical responsibility to advise against it and provide directive counseling by explaining why a cesarean delivery is medically necessary.

stem: A hospitalist who covers a cardiac ward in a tertiary care medical center notices that a hospital-based cardiologist, with whom she has worked for several years, is increasingly difficult to reach. The cardiologist now takes several hours to respond when he is paged while on call, appears distracted and irritable during discussions, and leaves his patient consult notes incomplete for longer than 48 hours. The hospitalist has also noticed that the cardiologist has been rounding at 11:00 PM; she once heard him mention "a family emergency" to one of the nurses. He has told the hospitalist that she can always call one of his partners as a backup if he does not answer pages. The hospitalist has not noticed any medical errors made by the cardiologist. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the hospitalist?

options.A: Ask the cardiologist's partners if they are aware of any trouble he is experiencing at home
options.B: Continue monitoring the cardiologist's performance for another month prior to determining appropriate action
options.C: Inquire among hospital staff whether they are concerned about the cardiologist's behavior
options.D: Inquire if there are any patient complaints filed against the cardiologist related to patient care
options.E: Report the cardiologist to the hospital Physician Health Program

explanations.A: Asking partners about the cardiologist's home life is professionally inappropriate and intrusive. Any suspected impairment should be formally investigated by the PHP, which can then implement steps for further evaluation and intervention as needed.
explanations.B: Once signs of suspected impairment have been observed, the hospitalist is ethically obligated to report. Waiting another month could potentially jeopardize patient safety and delay the opportunity for the cardiologist to receive needed treatment.
explanations.C: To protect patient safety and prevent potential future errors, a report should be made to the PHP, regardless of whether other hospital staff members are concerned or official patient complaints have been filed.
explanations.D: To protect patient safety and prevent potential future errors, a report should be made to the PHP, regardless of whether other hospital staff members are concerned or official patient complaints have been filed.

generalExplanation:
This cardiologist's behavior should raise concern for physician impairment, defined as impaired ability to practice medicine competently and safely. Signs of impairment include being increasingly difficult to reach, unusually late rounding times, decreased chart performance, and increased irritability and distractibility in clinical discussions. Deterioration in clinical performance is typically a late sign indicative of more severe impairment. Physicians are ethically obligated to report suspected physician impairment. |n the interests of patient safety and preventing medical errors, this should be done regardless of whether other staff has expressed similar concerns or patient complaints have been filed. Reports are made to Physician Health Programs (PHPs), which are typically hospital-based organizations designated to investigate reported concerns and arrange for a comprehensive assessment of the physician to help identify substance use and/or psychiatric/medical illness. If there is no designated PHP, the relevant chief of service should be informed.

PHPs are confidential resources that provide extensive support and expert education and monitoring. If intervention is required, the PHP can assist the physician in getting necessary treatment. Recovery rates are much higher than the general population, including among physicians involuntarily referred to PHPs, who generally express satisfication with their participation in the PHP. The majority of PHPs are independent from state medical boards, although, depending on the state, impaired physicians who choose not to follow PHP recommendations may be reported to the state medical board given the potential impact on public health and patient safety.
educationalObjective: Physicians are ethically obligated to report suspected physician impairment to protect patient safety. Physician Health Programs are organizations designated to investigate reported concerns and arrange for comprehensive assessment and treatment if necessary.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with essential hypertension, osteoarthritis, and major depressive disorder that is well controlled with cognitive behavioral therapy comes to the office due to 3 months of left knee pain. The pain is associated with 10 minutes of stiffness and swelling in the morning; it improves with heat or topical analgesic creams. The patient plays doubles tennis several evenings a week with a group of friends. She states that playing tennis is "part of my identity" and helps her cope with stress associated with her job as an investment banker. The patient has watched several online videos describing various knee pain treatments, including supplements, stem cell injections, and knee replacement. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 132/88 mm Hg, and pulse is 74/min. BMI is 29 kg/m². Examination shows mild tenderness to palpation of the knee joint, mild restriction of range of motion on the left knee compared with the right, and no swelling or palpable effusion. X-ray of the knee shows mild joint space narrowing with osteophytes. Which of the following actions should be prioritized first during this patient's visit?

options.A: Ascertaining whether the patient has been adherent to her blood pressure medication
options.B: Asking about the patient's interest in losing weight to improve her knee pain
options.C: Determining the patient's pain level and effect on her activities
options.D: Having the patient select her preferred knee pain treatment
options.E: Screening the patient for worsening symptoms of depression

explanations.A: Although this patient's other medical conditions (eg, hypertension, depression) should be monitored, her chief complaint of knee pain should be addressed first in this visit. Subsequently, depression screening, blood pressure monitoring, and medication reconciliation can be performed.
explanations.E: Although this patient's other medical conditions (eg, hypertension, depression) should be monitored, her chief complaint of knee pain should be addressed first in this visit. Subsequently, depression screening, blood pressure monitoring, and medication reconciliation can be performed.
explanations.B: Treatment recommendations, including weight loss, should be discussed only after patient-centered symptom assessment because this information will clarify treatment goals aligned with patient values.

PCC can be used to promote health care quality and treatments that align with patient priorities by: e measuring and tracking outcomes and information valued by patients (eg, pain level, functional status) as well as objective clinical data (eg, radiographic progression of disease).

e improving management of complex, chronic conditions (eg, pain management, cancer therapy), which often have multiple reasonable treatment approaches (eg, medications with various risk-benefit profiles, invasive treatment versus palliation).

This patient, who likely has knee osteoarthritis (minimal morning stiffness, osteophytes), strongly identifies with her ability to play tennis. The physician should first determine this patient's subjective experience of pain and how it has impacted her activities, as this information reflects patient priorities and should frame therapeutic discussions and goals (eg, return to playing tennis). After PCC-based assessment of her symptoms, treatment goals and recommendations can be selected through shared decision-making.

Shared decision-making optimizes care in chronic conditions featuring multiple reasonable management strategies (eg, pain management, cancer treatment), promoting selection of treatments aligned with patient priorities.

stem: A large tertiary care hospital in a major metropolitan area experiences a series of fatal medication errors involving excess doses of heparin in neonates. Multiple internal quality investigations reveal that, in addition to the medication errors, the hospital has experienced a higher-than-average frequency of near misses and adverse patient events involving diagnostic errors, iatrogenic infections, and documentation errors. A new chief medical officer is appointed and convenes an interdisciplinary quality and patient safety committee. The committee subsequently develops strategic recommendations to address the hospital's high incidence of adverse patient events. Which of the following committee recommendations is most likely to increase organizational safety and reduce the risk of patient harm?

options.A: Create workplace environments that increase reliance on human effort for correct action
options.B: Delegate safety oversight responsibilities to a specific group of health care personnel
options.C: Design workflow processes to minimize the consequences of incorrect actions
options.D: Perform event analyses routinely to identify personnel who are involved in errors Fee pea :
options.E: Promote clear organizational goals that target zero human errors in high-risk settings

explanations.A:
Although clear organizational goals and attention to individual effort (eg, vigilance, monitoring) are required for safety, even careful individuals may make errors in complex, distracting environments. Therefore, organizational goals of zero human errors are unrealistic, do not address errors latent within systems, and can promote a culture of fear. Instead, organizations should set goals of zero adverse events (ie, no harm to patients) that can be facilitated through systems and processes that reduce, not increase, reliance on human effort (eg, reduce reliance on memory by using checklists and standardized processes).

generalExplanation:
Errors that cause serious patient harm (eg, fatal medication errors) occur with unacceptable frequency in health care settings. To improve patient safety, health care systems can emulate high-reliability organizations (HROs) (eg, aviation industry). These organizations minimize catastrophic errors despite operating in complex, high- hazard environments like health care. HROs build a culture of safety through a systems approach to error prevention. This approach is characterized by: e Resilience to error: This approach views human error as inevitable in complex settings and designs workflow processes (eg, standardization, adding double-checks) that anticipate and minimize the consequences of such errors (eg, preprogrammed dosing limits on a drug infusion pump that minimize the potential patient harm from a staff member accidentally entering an excessive drug dose). e« Comprehensive analysis: This approach avoids simplistic explanations for errors (eg, focusing only on individual personnel). It carefully examines all factors, including latent factors (eg, system-level vulnerabilities) (Choice D).

• Team-based vigilance: This approach assigns safety oversight responsibilities to all individuals; each team member continuously monitors for errors and may speak candidly without fear of retaliation (Choice B).

stem: A 73-year-old woman is seen in the hospital following emergent left ttansmetatarsal amputation. The patient has a history of chronic, nonhealing foot ulcers due to poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and peripheral artery disease and was admitted 2 days ago with wet gangrene and cellulitis. At the time of admission, she had fever, hypotension, and altered mental status, and consent for amputation was provided by her son who is her designated surrogate decision maker. Following surgery, the patient has been stabilized with intravenous antibiotics, opioid pain medications, and appropriate thromboembolism prophylaxis. When the vascular surgeon explains his recommendation for left lower extremity angiography and possible revascularization to prevent further amputation, the patient refuses the procedures. She says, "I'm too old for another operation. I didn't want surgery the first time, and I don't want it now." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

options.A: Ask the patient's son for consent to perform the procedure
options.B: Assess the patient for depressive symptoms
options.C: Check to see if the patient has a living will
options.D: Determine if the patient has capacity to refuse the procedure
options.E: Document the patient's refusal and do not perform the procedure
options.F: Obtain two-physician consent to perform the procedure

explanations.A: These options can only be considered if a capacity reassessment determines that the patient still lacks decision-making capacity. If the patient has regained capacity to make decisions, her wishes supersede the wishes of the son or any instructions documented previously in a living will.
explanations.C: These options can only be considered if a capacity reassessment determines that the patient still lacks decision-making capacity. If the patient has regained capacity to make decisions, her wishes supersede the wishes of the son or any instructions documented previously in a living will.
explanations.B: Assessment of the patient's decision-making capacity is the critical determinant of the next step in her medical management. If her capacity is in question, then it is reasonable to determine if depression is affecting her judgment.
explanations.E: This patient was recently incapacitated. Assessment and documentation that she has regained capacity should be performed before accepting her decision as an informed refusal.
explanations.F: Two-physician consent is used in some states when there is no living will or surrogate available to make decisions for a patient without capacity.

generalExplanation:
This patient's mental status has improved; however, it is not clear whether she has fully regained capacity to make her own health care decisions. Although it was appropriate for her son to act as a surrogate decision maker to consent for the amputation when she was clearly incapacitated, the patient is now refusing further procedures. The most appropriate next step is to reassess her decision-making capacity. Factors potentially affecting her cognition such as delirium (due to infection or metabolic derangements) and cognitive effects of opioid pain medication should be considered. If the patient has regained capacity, her decision must be respected and supersede the wishes of any surrogate decision maker.

superseae tne wishes of any surrogate aecision Maker.

Components of capacity include understanding the condition, ability to express a choice, appreciation of the consequences of treatment options (including no treatment), and ability to provide reasoning for the decision. If the patient meets these criteria, it is her right to refuse treatment.
educationalObjective: Incapacitated patients may regain capacity as their condition improves. These patients should be reassessed for capacity before health care decisions are made.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with a history of mild cognitive impairment, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension is brought to the emergency department by her daughter after sustaining a fall. The patient's daughter, a full-time nurse who visits her mother daily, found her confused and lying on the ground. The daughter checked her mother's blood sugar and found it to be 55 mg/dL. After the patient drank some apple juice, the confusion quickly improved. The patient takes 10 different medications, including insulin and an antidepressant, which was recently prescribed by her neurologist for symptoms of apathy. Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 127/86 mm Hg, and pulse is 78/min. She is alert and oriented to self, time, and place. Physical examination shows tenderness of the right ankle but is otherwise normal. Repeat fingerstick glucose is 85 mg/dL. The patient is treated for ankle sprain and can ambulate with a cane and her ankle in a boot. The pain is controlled. The patient lives alone in a single- story home, is independent with activities of daily living, and was seen in the emergency department 5 months ago for a similar episode. She requests to go home, but her daughter expresses concern about her mother's ability to take medications as prescribed. In addition to close primary care follow-up, which of the following interventions is most recommended to prevent future recurrence of falls in this patient?

options.A: Admit the patient to the hospital for cognitive and functional Set
options.B: Arrange for the patient to receive home health care
options.C: Request that the patient's daughter administer her medications at home
options.D: Transfer the patient to a skilled nursing facility until her ankle heals

explanations.A: Admitting this patient when she is medically stable for discharge is not recommended because it increases her risk for adverse events (eg, nosocomial infections) and represents inefficient resource use. Cognitive assessments can be performed in the home and at follow-up appointments.
explanations.D: Skilled nursing facilities are appropriate when patients cannot live at home or require continuous monitoring (eg, post-stroke rehabilitation, severe cognitive impairment). Although this patient may eventually require a skilled nursing facility if her cognitive function worsens, she currently has only mild cognitive impairment and minor ankle injury. Therefore, primary care follow-up and home health physical therapy is preferred to reduce her fall risk while preserving her independence.

generalExplanation:
Falls are a major cause of morbidity in the elderly. This patient, who likely fell due to hypoglycemia from insulin use, is now medically stable for discharge (ie, ambulates with assistance, is normoglycemic). However, she has risk factors for future falls, including new ankle injury, complex medication regimen, previous fall history, age, and cognitive impairment. Fall risk reduction for this patient is best achieved through home health care, which describes home-based, interdisciplinary care (eg, physical therapy, nursing) provided by skilled professionals (eg, nurses, licensed social workers).

As a form of care coordination (ie, facilitating safe transition of care), home health care increases health care quality (eg, reducing hospital readmissions and medication errors). It is preferred for this patient due to the following: e She will be home-bound from ankle injury and continue to have medical needs, including physical therapy and medication management (eg, safe insulin administration) to reduce hypoglycemia risk. e She can receive a home safety assessment (eg, by an occupational therapist) to identify environmental fall risk factors (eg, throw rugs, no handrails in bathtub).

e She lives independently and expresses preference to return home; her autonomy, independence, and mental health can be promoted safely through home health care. When possible, optimizing home safety and engaging patients directly are preferred to relying on visiting family members, such as the patient's daughter who has a full-time job (Choice C).
educationalObjective: Home health care, a form of care coordination (eg, safe transition of care), provides home-based, interdisciplinary health services (eg, physical therapy, home safety assessment, management of complex medication regimen) by skilled professionals (eg, nurses, social workers). It improves safety (eg, reducing fall risk in the elderly) and health care quality while maintaining patient independence, autonomy, and engagement.

stem:
The medical director of a busy primary care clinic is leading a quality-improvement project aimed at reducing the patient no-show rate. The director is planning to implement a telephone and text-messaging reminder service that sends a message to patients 1 day prior to their appointment, prompting them to confirm their appointment or reschedule.

Which of the following quality-improvement strategies is best suited to systematically assess this reminder system's effectiveness on no-show rates?

options.A: Conducting a near-miss analysis after system implementation
options.B: Constructing a run chart analyzing longitudinal trends
options.C: Distributing patient and staff surveys pre- and post-system implementation
options.D: Performing a failure modes and effects analysis a

explanations.A: Anear-miss analysis is used following a "close call," an event that could have resulted in patient harm but was prevented in time, such as when an incorrect medication dose is ordered for a patient, but the error is detected by the nurse before administration.
explanations.C: Staff and patient surveys may provide useful information on reminder system acceptability; however, run charts offer superior assessment of system effectiveness because they directly track the outcome of interest (no-show rate).
explanations.D: Failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA) is a prospective quality improvement tool in which an error-prone process (eg, central line insertion) is analyzed to determine all mechanisms, or "modes" (eg, incorrect sterile procedure), causing error (eg, infections). FMEA would not provide useful information on no-show rates or the reminder system's effectiveness.

generalExplanation: A run chart is a longitudinal graph that tracks a process performance outcome (eg, patient no-show rates, a metric of patient follow-up and scheduling efficiency) over time. Run charts are frequently used to: e Visually identify performance variations, including trends, defined as a consistent directional change (eg, increase or decrease) for 25 consecutive points e Assess effectiveness of a quality improvement intervention by comparing changes in process outcomes pre- and post-intervention A run chart is appropriate for assessing this reminder system's potential effectiveness in improving no-show rates. Assuming absence of other concurrent interventions, a downward trend in no-show rates following implementation suggests that the system likely helped reduce no-show rates.
