The medical director of a busy primary care clinic is leading a quality-improvement project aimed at reducing the patient no-show rate. The director is planning to implement a telephone and text-messaging reminder service that sends a message to patients 1 day prior to their appointment, prompting them to confirm their appointment or reschedule.

The medical director tracks monthly no-show rates for 18 months following implementation of the reminder system. A run chart is constructed comparing no-show rates prior to and following system implementation, as shown below. Which of the following conclusions is most closely supported by the trends seen in the run chart?

options.A: The reminder system caused sufficient improvement in patient follow-up rates
options.B: The reminder system failed to produce meaningful improvements in patient follow-up
options.C: The reminder system addresses some, but not all, causes of low patient follow-up
options.D: Patient follow-up outcomes appear independent of reminder system effects
options.E: Potential effectiveness of the reminder system cannot be determined by the data shown

explanations.D: The graph shows a consistent downward trend in post-system no-show rates that was absent pre- intervention, suggesting that no-show rates were influenced by the system (rather than being independent).
explanations.E: The decreasing trend in no-show rates following implementation supports the system's partial effectiveness in reducing no-show rates.

generalExplanation:
Run charts, a graph of an outcome of interest (eg, no-show rates) over time, are often used to assess effectiveness of a quality improvement intervention (eg, reminder system). This run chart suggests that the reminder system was partially effective in reducing no-show rates: e Prior to the intervention, no-show rates are unacceptably high for all data points (ie, markedly above goal rate of 10%).

e Following the intervention, no-show rates follow a downward trend, with consistently decreasing no-show rates from months June to October (ie, for 25 consecutive points) (Choice B).

e No show-rates meet or perform better than the goal at several instances.

However, the run chart also indicates that the reminder system has not consistently achieved sufficient no-show reductions. For example, no-show rates are still unacceptably high during certain months (eg, November, December) (Choice A).

Therefore, based on the run chart's findings, the reminder system likely addresses some factors reducing patient follow-up (eg, patient forgetting appointment) but not others (eg, seasonal travel for end-of-year holidays).
educationalObjective: Run charts enable systematic assessment of an intervention's effect on process performance (eg, no-show rate). Presence of a desired trend (ie, consistent directional change for 5 or more data points in a row) post-intervention suggests potential effectiveness; persistent underperformance or excessive variation suggests the intervention only partially addresses factors influencing performance.

stem: A survey is conducted among medical residents at a busy academic medical center to assess resident experiences regarding handoff errors. The survey finds that 87% of residents report at least 1 adverse event affecting patient care due to inadequate handoffs; these adverse events are most common between 11:00 PM and 5:00 AM, when a cross-covering resident manages care of patients belonging to multiple primary teams. In addition to system-level strategies, which of the following practices is most effective in reducing the risk for adverse events resulting from verbal handoffs?

options.A: Encourage questions only at the end of the handoff discussion
options.B: Focus on severely ill patients at the beginning of the handoff
options.C: Discourage note-taking during the discussion to increase attentiveness
options.D: Provide thorough detail on the clinical status and course of every patient SS... = = = ————————————————————_—

explanations.C: Note-taking should be encouraged during the discussion; it can emphasize and help reinforce important information exchanged during the hand-off.
explanations.D: Although handoffs should include additional details (eg, clinical course, baseline status) relating to critically ill patients, providing thorough detail on the clinical status of every patient is not recommended because this can lead to information overload and overwhelm the receiver.

generalExplanation:
Handoffs (also called sign-outs) involve oral and written information exchange to facilitate the transfer of patient care (eg, from primary team to cross-covering resident or new service). Handoffs increase the risk for communication errors and patient adverse events; such errors are more common when handoffs involve many patients or multiple high-acuity patients.

Handoffs necessitate communicating a large amount of information in limited time. Errors can be reduced by — eS ae eae Vere ee ae ae ee re Handoffs (also called sign-outs) involve oral and written information exchange to facilitate the transfer of patient care (eg, from primary team to cross-covering resident or new service). Handoffs increase the risk for communication errors and patient adverse events; such errors are more common when handoffs involve many patients or multiple high-acuity patients.

Handoffs necessitate communicating a large amount of information in limited time. Errors can be reduced by prioritizing information, which reduces information overload. Communication should focus first on severely ill patients who have the highest risk for complications or unforeseen clinical deterioration (eg, diabetic ketoacidosis, high-risk labor and delivery). For these patients, information on daily clinical progress and baseline clinical status should be communicated at the beginning of the handoff, along with clear anticipatory guidance (eg, "if/then" instructions regarding possible clinical scenarios).

The following are additional best practices for handoffs: e Follow a structured format (eg, checklist) to ensure that basic information (eg, code status) is consistently covered.

e Adopt an interactive approach, encouraging the receiver to ask questions and clarify items throughout the discussion, rather than only at the end, which increases the risk of rushing or forgetting questions (Choice A). e Perform selective read-back (ie, closed-loop communication in which the receiver repeats back the information to ensure accurate comprehension) of the most critical information.
educationalObjective: Verbal handoffs during transfers of care necessitate exchanging a large amount of information in a limited time. To minimize communication errors, handoff discussions should prioritize patients with highest medical acuity, confirm accurate comprehension of critical information (eg, selective read-back), and follow a structured and interactive approach.

stem: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother for evaluation of recent behavioral changes. The patient has been sleeping poorly and recently started wetting her bed. Her grades in school have dropped significantly, and she has been notably anxious and sad. The patient's parents are having financial difficulties and considering divorce. The father drinks alcohol most evenings after coming home from work. The mother appears stressed by her husband's drinking and is very concerned about her daughter. The physician has known the patient since she was a toddler and found her to be cheerful, lively, and cooperative at her checkup 6 months ago. After the mother leaves the room, the physician asks the patient about school and home, at which point she suddenly bursts into tears. After providing support, which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

options.A: Ask the patient about physical, emotional, or sexual abuse
options.B: Encourage the mother to attend a support group for family members of alcoholics
options.C: Interview the mother alone
options.D: Reassure patient and mother that this is a normal stress response
options.E: Recommend cognitive-behavioral therapy

explanations.B: Although encouraging the mother to attend a support group and initiating family therapy may be helpful, these would not take priority over assessing the patient for abuse.
explanations.F: Although encouraging the mother to attend a support group and initiating family therapy may be helpful, these would not take priority over assessing the patient for abuse.
explanations.C: It is important to speak with the mother alone to get further details about the home environment, which she may not wish to reveal in front of her daughter. However, this does not take precedence over completing the interview with the patient and assessing for abuse.
explanations.D: Changes in behavior and mood often occur in normal children in response to common psychosocial stressors such as divorce or parental discord. However, abuse must also be ruled out when a child has abrupt changes in mood, bedwetting, and academic decline.
explanations.E: Cognitive-behavioral therapy has been studied for a number of psychological disorders in children and adolescents. Although it may have a role in the long-term management of this patient, psychotherapy would be a secondary priority and should not delay the urgent need to exclude abuse.

generalExplanation:
When working with vulnerable patients such as children, it is imperative that physicians be alert to any signs of possible abuse. Abuse must be ruled out in any child with abrupt onset of mood changes, bedwetting, and/or academic difficulties. Other factors associated with increased risk of abuse in this child include unstable family situation, financial difficulties, and caregiver history of substance abuse.

Physical, sexual and emotional abuse should be considered early when evaluating mood and behavioral symptoms in children due to the high risk of recurrent abuse and the need for prompt intervention. The physician should ask the parent(s) to leave the room and provide a safe environment for the child to talk about her feelings and concerns. If abuse is confirmed or there remains a high index of suspicion of abuse, the physician is mandated to report it.
educationalObjective: Physicians should have a high suspicion for abuse in children with sudden changes in mood, behavior, or academic work, as well as in children with stressful family environments or parents with active drug/alcohol abuse.

stem: A 45-year-old man is seen in a home visit for follow-up of advanced melanoma with brain metastasis. He is bed- bound and requires 2-person assistance for all transfers. The patient has been enrolled in hospice for the past 3 months after multiple curative attempts failed, and his condition has declined significantly. His oncologist estimates that death is likely within 2-4 weeks. The patient says, "My daughter is getting married in 4 months, and I would really like to be there when it happens." Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient's statement?

options.A: "I wish you could stay alive until the wedding, but I worry you may not. Maybe you can consider creating a symbol of your presence, like a letter that can be shared at the wedding."
options.B: "If attending the wedding is your goal, then I would recommend that you withdraw from hospice care for another attempt at aggressive treatment."
options.C: "It is always possible that a miracle can happen. I will always be here for you and hope that you will make it to the wedding."
options.D: "There is still a chance you will survive to your daughter's wedding. But we cannot control nature, and your time will likely come before then."
options.E: "Unfortunately, it is unlikely that you will live that long. I encourage you to arrange a meeting with your daughter now and anyone else you wish to say your final goodbyes." submit

explanations.B: Although a patient may withdraw from hospice to pursue life-prolonging treatment, this patient has not expressed a desire to do so. Multiple treatment attempts have already failed, and encouraging such a course may lead to treatment complications with little chance of benefit.
explanations.C: This statement conveys optimism but provides no constructive way for the patient to achieve his goal. It also does not recognize the patient's poor prognosis and may encourage false hope.
explanations.D: Although these statements avoid false hope and communicate realistic information, neither encourages the patient to consider reframing his goal (ie, being present at the wedding) through alternate means.
explanations.E: Although these statements avoid false hope and communicate realistic information, neither encourages the patient to consider reframing his goal (ie, being present at the wedding) through alternate means.

generalExplanation: Patients with terminal illness often have difficulty achieving desired goals due to intractable symptoms (eg, pain, nausea), impaired function, or reduced life expectancy. In such cases, physicians should encourage patients to reframe their goals in more attainable ways. Conveying difficult information using a "wish...worry" or "hope... worry" framework (ie, "I wish you could stay alive for the wedding, but I worry you may not") can be effective. Additional recommended steps include: e Exploring the patient's current understanding of the disease, prognosis, and functional limitations e Clarifying the patient's priorities and values to specify what the patient wishes to achieve and why e Expressing empathy tempered by a realistic assessment of disease status and avoiding false hope e Gently offering constructive suggestions, such as an alternate approach or revised timing, to help the patient regain some control and cope with grief This patient has a poor prognosis and may not live to see his daughter's wedding. The physician can empathetically assist the patient in reframing his goal of being present at the wedding, by reiterating prognosis using a "wish...worry" statement, and suggesting an alternate approach for participation (eg, creating a symbol, such as a letter).
educationalObjective: Physicians can approach difficult conversations about prognosis and express empathy to patients using a "wish... worry" framework (eg, "I wish you could stay alive much longer, but I worry you may not"). Physicians should clarify patient priorities, avoid promoting false hope, and offer constructive suggestions to help patients reframe their goals in more attainable, realistic ways.

stem: A group of researchers at an academic medical center are conducting research on implicit bias in 200 emergency medicine trainees. A survey is administered, asking respondents to agree or disagree with the following statements: "I believe in offering equitable care to patients regardless of ethnicity"; "My patients' ethnicity does not influence my quality of care." One hundred percent of respondents agree with both statements. Subsequently, a computerized implicit bias test is administered. The test displays images of faces from either a minority or nonminority ethnic group, alongside a list of positive or negative words, such as "cooperative," "noncompliant," or "drug-seeking." Respondents are asked to quickly match one word to each face, and differences in response times for positive or negative associations by ethnicity are measured. Results show 76% of respondents more rapidly associate the minority ethnicity with "noncompliant" and "drug-seeking." Which of the following is the best next step?

options.A: Create an anonymous portal to report instances of witnessed discrimination
options.B: Generate organizational guidelines emphasizing a zero-tolerance policy against discrimination
options.C: No action is strictly necessary because all trainees demonstrate explicit belief in equitable care
options.D: Organize interactive group debriefing sessions to discuss aggregate study results
options.E: Remediate trainees displaying the most rapid negative associations with ethnic minority images

explanations.A: Anonymous error-reporting portals are important but address only visible, overt discrimination, which is not evident in this study. Portals are less likely to detect or address implicit bias, which exerts subtle, less visible influences on provider-patient interactions (eg, spending less time with a patient of a group perceived to be noncompliant).
explanations.B: Organizational guidelines can promote a culture of health equity; however, as seen in this study, providers often believe they already offer equitable care (despite having implicit bias). Moreover, providers are often unaware of how their unconscious attitudes influence care outcomes. Therefore, small group debriefing is a superior next step in promoting awareness and discussion of implicit bias.
explanations.E: Providers are often unaware of their implicit biases and can experience distress upon discovery. Therefore, organizations should avoid punitive actions and focus on increasing collaborative (eg, small group) discussion and awareness.

generalExplanation:
Implicit bias describes subconscious alterations in thoughts and attitudes toward specific groups (eg, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, age). As seen in this study, implicit bias contrasts with explicit discrimination: All respondents (100%) consciously expressed commitment to equity, but 76% demonstrated unconscious, implicit bias by more rapidly associating faces belonging to the ethnic minority group with negative words (eg, "drug- seeking"). Implicit bias perpetuates health disparities by subtly but systematically altering provider-patient interactions (eg, communication style, diagnostic workup); therefore, organizational action addressing implicit bias is indicated (Choice C).

According to the Joint Commission, implicit bias can be addressed by the following measures: e Assess for bias: Implicit bias uses heuristics (eg, fast thinking or mental shortcuts); therefore, it is frequently measured using rapid image association tests (eg, Implicit Association Test), as described in this study. e Encourage awareness and collaborative discussion of implicit biases: In this case, group debriefing on the study results is the best next step.

e Train clinicians in metacognition (ie, self-monitoring cognitive patterns): This process can reduce automatic, unconscious reliance on stereotypes and flawed patterns (common in complex, busy settings).
educationalObjective: Implicit bias, or subconscious attitudes toward specific groups (eg, ethnicity), is highly prevalent and can perpetuate health disparities. Organizations can address implicit bias by assessing for its presence, encouraging individual and group awareness (eg, small group debriefing), and promoting metacognition (ie, self-monitoring thought processes).

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the office by his grandmother for a new patient visit. The boy has a known diagnosis of HIV infection acquired perinatally from his mother and has been taking highly active antiretroviral medications since infancy. The grandmother is the patient's legal guardian; his mother died from complications of AIDS several years ago. While the patient is having his vital signs measured, the grandmother explains that she has not revealed the diagnosis to the patient because she wants "to let him live a normal childhood." Although the patient has been compliant with his HIV medications, he believes they are vitamins. Vital signs are normal. Weight is at the 45th percentile for age. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. Viral load is undetectable with a CD4 lymphocyte count of 780 cells/mm³. Speaking privately with the pediatrician after the examination, the grandmother reiterates that she does not want to disclose the patient's diagnosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: "Ethically, I cannot continue seeing him without letting him know why."
options.B: "I agree he should have a normal childhood, and I'll continue telling him his medications are vitamins."
options.C: "I won't discuss the diagnosis with him, but you're obligated to tell him in the near future."
options.D: "If we don't tell him, he's going to find out on his own, and it may ruin your relationship."
options.E: "We don't have to tell him his diagnosis today, but we need a plan to explain it to him soon."

explanations.A: Discontinuing care that is medically necessary is inappropriate and harmful to the patient.
explanations.B: Failure to address the need for diagnosis disclosure increases the risk of infection transmission and medication noncompliance.
explanations.D: Coercing disclosure through threats creates distrust and harms the relationship between the family and the provider.

generalExplanation:
Persons with perinatally acquired HIV infection are now living longer into adulthood due to advances in antiretroviral therapy. Parents and guardians of children living with HIV often avoid disclosing the diagnosis to them in an attempt to preserve normal childhood experiences. Other common fears associated with diagnosis disclosure include concern for a changing family dynamic and worry over the parents' HIV statuses becoming public.

Adolescence is a period when developmental maturation is associated with increasing autonomy. Adolescents may ask questions about their own health and begin exploring sexuality. For this reason, it is recommended that children know and understand their HIV diagnosis by adolescence. Disclosure at this time fosters trust and autonomy, increases medication compliance, and decreases the risk of unknowingly transmitting the virus. However, it is appropriate to respect family members' concerns and give them time to prepare themselves for the potential emotional and psychological responses. The provider should encourage the family to develop a plan with a timeline for the conversation to occur. The discussion with the patient is a process that involves joint participation between the family and the provider using open-ended questions and offering support to the patient. The full burden of how to disclose serious information should not fall on the family, particularly in cases of chronic disease with increased morbidity and mortality rates (Choice C).
educationalObjective: Disclosure of an HIV diagnosis to a child with perinatally acquired infection should occur by adolescence to foster patient autonomy, increase medication compliance, and prevent transmission. The provider should respect the family's concerns and offer joint participation in establishing a timeline and plan for disclosure.

stem: An unconscious 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after sustaining a gunshot wound to the chest during an attempted robbery at a convenience store. He is bleeding profusely. The patient is minimally responsive to pain and is unable to provide any history. The ambulance record indicates that his initial blood pressure was 120/70 mm Hg, pulse was 95/min, and respirations were 16/min. The patient's current blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg, pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 28/min. He has an open gunshot wound in the chest and an exit wound in the back. Intravenous fluids and vasopressors are started, and a blood transfusion is ordered. The patient's fiancé arrives and states that he should not receive a blood transfusion because he is a devout Jehovah's Witness. No evidence is found in the medical chart of advance directives or a living will documenting the patient's wishes, and examination of his belongings show no blood refusal card. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

options.A: Administer high-dose erythropoietin and intravenous iron to stabilize blood loss
options.B: Continue intravenous fluids and consult the hospital ethics committee
options.C: Obtain a court order for approval to administer the blood transfusion
options.D: Proceed with the blood transfusion
options.E: Withhold the blood transfusion because of the patient's religious beliefs

explanations.A: Case reports have shown some success in using high-dose erythropoietin, crystalloids, intravenous iron, and other products to address massive hemorrhage without a blood transfusion. These treatments could be discussed if the patient was conscious and refused a blood transfusion.
explanations.B: Ethics committees provide advice if disagreements or ambiguity exist between health care providers and a patient/patient's family on decisions involving withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatments. This patient needs treatment quickly, with no time for discussion with the ethics committee.
explanations.C: Court approval is not needed for a physician to proceed with emergency life-saving treatment for an unconscious or unresponsive patient.

generalExplanation: This patient is a presumed Jehovah's Witness who presents with hemorrhagic shock and is likely to benefit from a transfusion that could prevent exsanguination. Because the patient lacks decision-making capacity, providers should determine if he has completed an advance directive that can guide treatment decisions. Most Jehovah's Witnesses carry advance directive cards that explicitly document the individual's refusal of a blood transfusion. In the case of adult patients, courts have consistently supported the right to refuse blood on religious grounds. In this case, no advance directive card is provided and delay in treatment could place the patient in serious harm. The Health Care Consent Act has been applied to Jehovah's Witnesses to allow transfusion to preserve a patient's life in an emergency when no blood refusal card is present. The patient's fiancé is not a legal next of kin and cannot serve as a substituted decision-maker (Choice E).
educationalObjective: In the absence of an advance directive, a life-saving blood transfusion can be given to a Jehovah's Witness who lacks decision-making capacity.

stem: A 59-year-old man comes to the office for a preventive visit. He feels well but has experienced an unexpected 2.3 kg (5 Ib) weight loss in the last 2 months. The patient has a 40-pack-year smoking history, and medical history is otherwise unremarkable. Physical examination is normal. Fecal occult blood testing is positive and colonoscopy is advised. The patient asks, "A colonoscopy, that sounds serious! Do you think I have cancer?" Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient's question?

options.A: "Colonoscopy is routine in these situations. We can discuss this more accurately once we have the results."
options.B: "I| am not sure what is wrong, but that is the reason we need a colonoscopy."
options.C: "I suspect that you have cancer of the colon, and colonoscopy is the best way to confirm that."
options.D: "There are several possibilities, some of which are potentially serious. A colonoscopy is the best way to know for sure."
options.E: "You probably have cancer, but I will be here to help you through it, no matter what."

explanations.A: Colonoscopy is routine for patients with a positive fecal occult blood test. However, this statement does not explain why it is necessary or encourage shared decision-making.
explanations.B: Expressing uncertainty is appropriate. However, this statement is unnecessarily vague, and uncertainty alone does not justify invasive testing.
explanations.C: Discussing life-changing conditions (eg, cancer, dementia) requires tact. Although the possibility of serious disease should not be hidden from a patient, blunt and direct statements such as this can be alarming and are more appropriate when specific features (eg, lytic bone lesions, visible mass on CT) make a benign diagnosis unlikely. This patient's symptoms are suspicious but highly nonspecific.
explanations.E: Although this statement includes an appropriate expression of concern and support, it is unnecessarily alarming and does not lead to discussion of the necessary plan of care with the patient.

generalExplanation: This patient with a significant smoking history has unexplained weight loss and a positive fecal occult blood test, which together suggest a possible malignancy in the colon. This presentation warrants further evaluation with colonoscopy, which should be completed in a timely manner. However, the patient's clinical features are not specific for malignancy, and there is significant uncertainty as to the cause of his symptoms. However, the patient's clinical features are not specific for malignancy, and there is significant uncertainty as to the cause of his symptoms. Counseling this patient should include a clear statement that his symptoms could represent a serious condition; the conversation need not detail every possibility in the differential diagnosis, but the clinician's suspicion should be explained in a way that the individual patient can understand. The clinician should also convey an appropriate sense of clinical uncertainty. In this particular case, the level of uncertainty is high, which should be expressed to the patient. The plan for diagnostic tests and subsequent follow-up should be as clear and specific as possible (eg, "I will call you with test results on Monday"). Finally, the patient should have adequate opportunity to ask questions and obtain clarification.
educationalObjective: Counseling a patient in the setting of clinical uncertainty should convey the potential seriousness of the situation and include an individualized discussion of differential diagnosis based on known facts of the case. The degree of uncertainty should be acknowledged. The discussion should also explain the need for further evaluation, include a clear plan for follow-up, and allow the patient an opportunity to ask questions.

stem: A 75-year-old woman with dementia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease is transferred to the hospital due to shortness of breath that manifested during dialysis. The patient is diagnosed with pneumonia; broad-spectrum antibiotics are begun, and dialysis is continued in the hospital. However, her condition deteriorates, and she experiences multiple organ system failure. The patient's nephrologist believes that withdrawing dialysis is the most appropriate action. On discussing this possibility with the patient's daughter, she becomes upset and says, "I feel like I will be a bad daughter if I give up on her now." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: "Although you are doing the best you can, sometimes it is better to let our loved ones go rather than let them suffer."
options.B: "Help me understand what your mother was like before she got sick, and we can decide what course is most appropriate for her together."
options.C: "I know this is hard, but I trust that you are putting your mother's best interests first and will respect whatever decision you make."
options.D: "Instead of thinking that you are giving up, be comforted that you are helping your mother achieve a peaceful death."
options.E: "You are a good daughter as long as you honor what your mother would have wanted most in this situation."

explanations.A: These statements express empathy but emphasize the difficulty of the daughter's decision instead of the patient's goals and values. Rather than easing the decision, these options may be seen as paternalistic and increase conflict between the physician and the daughter.
explanations.D: These statements express empathy but emphasize the difficulty of the daughter's decision instead of the patient's goals and values. Rather than easing the decision, these options may be seen as paternalistic and increase conflict between the physician and the daughter.
explanations.C: The daughter is struggling with guilt associated with a difficult decision. This statement offers passive encouragement but places the burden of the decision entirely on the daughter, without attempting to assist her in working through it.
explanations.E: This statement invokes substituted judgment but places excessive pressure on the patient's daughter (ie, she is a good daughter only if she honors her mother's wishes). Keeping the focus clearly on the patient's goals and values, rather than the daughter's worthiness, is more likely to facilitate effective decision-making.

generalExplanation:
This patient has a grave prognosis and is a potential candidate for withdrawal of care. However, surrogate decision-makers, such as this patient's daughter, commonly experience stress (eg, "being a bad daughter"), grief (eg, "giving up"), and conflict when considering withdrawal of care.

Physicians can assist distressed surrogate decision-makers by guiding them in applying substituted judgment (ie, acting on what the patient would have wanted rather than the decision-maker's feelings or preferences). The following techniques may be helpful: e Refocus the discussion on the patient, by asking what the patient was like before the illness. This step brings attention to the patient's goals and values and builds trust between the physician and surrogate. e Help surrogates apply their knowledge of the patient's goals to the current situation using objective clinical information (eg, prognosis, potential complications).

e Emphasize shared decision-making. The physician should offer close, empathetic guidance and make recommendations based on the patient's medical condition and information shared about the patient. This step can reduce the burden of decision-making for the surrogate and alleviate feelings of guilt.
educationalObjective: Surrogate decision-makers can experience significant emotional distress when making decisions associated with end-of-life care. Physicians can assist surrogates by refocusing discussions on patients' goals and values (ie, substituted judgment) and providing close, empathetic guidance in shared decision-making.

stem: Administrators at a tertiary care hospital are evaluating approaches to reduce in-hospital patient mortality rates outside the intensive care unit. An analysis of recent patient deaths due to cardiac arrest reveals potentially preventable contributing factors, including delays in recognizing or responding efficiently to deterioration in patient clinical status. Which of the following interventions is recommended to improve outcomes for patients at risk for sudden cardiac arrest in this hospital?

options.A: Conducting an assessment of burnout and fatigue among hospital staff in multiple departments
options.B: Designating an interprofessional team to regularly monitor patients who have concerning clinical signs
options.C: Developing an alert system that pages the unit charge nurse each time a patient develops abnormal vital signs
options.D: Hiring additional hospital staff and increasing the number of beds in the hospital
options.E: Reducing the length of shifts worked by physicians and nurses

explanations.A: Staff burnout, which can increase fatigue and risk of error, should be assessed regularly. However, RRTs are more likely to practically improve clinical management of high-risk patients and can potentially reduce staff burnout by sharing the primary care teams' workload (eg, monitoring and treating the highest-risk patients).
explanations.C: Automated alert systems can notify providers of deterioration in a patient's clinical status. However, to be effective, an alert system should involve parameters that are specific for signs of high-risk clinical deterioration. In contrast, excessive notifications (eg, each time a patient develops an abnormal vital sign) can cause desensitization to alerts and lead to missing warning signals of significant events (ie, alarm fatigue).
explanations.D: Increasing the number of staff and beds without improving the systems to manage high-risk patients is unlikely to change outcomes.
explanations.E: Extended shifts can lead to fatigue and associated errors. However, reducing shift length requires more frequent changes in care teams (ie, handoffs), which can increase the chance of complications for high-risk patients. Dedicating a team to support monitoring and management is more likely to improve clinical outcomes.

generalExplanation:
Busy hospitals often experience delays in recognizing and responding to acute deterioration in patients' clinical status. Rapid response teams (RRTs) can provide early intervention in case of clinical decline, and their use is associated with improved patient outcomes (eg, reduced incidence of cardiac arrest and associated mortality). RRTs are characterized by the following: e Multidisciplinary team: RRTs typically include practitioners from multiple health professions, including nurses, physicians, and respiratory therapists.

e Patient assessment: RRTs support primary care teams by regularly monitoring patients who are at high risk of clinical decline. RRTs can assess and immediately treat patients when signs of clinical deterioration appear, preventing serious sequelae.

• Activation criteria: RRTs are typically activated based on early clinical warning signs manifested by the patient (eg, sustained tachypnea, arrhythmia, uncontrolled pain).
educationalObjective: Multidisciplinary rapid response teams provide clinical assessment and early intervention for hospitalized patients at high risk for clinical deterioration. Such teams can support primary care teams and reduce in-hospital mortality rates.
